verses.text: Yahweh’s word which came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the nations.

Of Egypt: concerning the army of Pharaoh Necoh king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates in Carchemish, which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon struck in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah.
“Prepare the buckler and shield, and draw near to battle!
Harness the horses, and get up, you horsemen, and stand up with your helmets. Polish the spears, put on the coats of mail.
Why have I seen it? They are dismayed and are turned backward. Their mighty ones are beaten down, have fled in haste, and don’t look back. Terror is on every side,” says Yahweh.
“Don’t let the swift flee away, nor the mighty man escape. In the north by the river Euphrates they have stumbled and fallen.
“Who is this who rises up like the Nile, whose waters toss themselves like the rivers?
Egypt rises up like the Nile, and his waters toss themselves like the rivers: and he says, ‘I will rise up, I will cover the earth. I will destroy cities and its inhabitants.’
Go up, you horses; and rage, you chariots! Let the mighty men go out: Cush and Put, who handle the shield; and the Ludim, who handle and bend the bow.

For that day is of the Lord, Yahweh of Armies, a day of vengeance, that he may avenge himself of his adversaries. The sword will devour and be satiated, and will drink its fill of their blood; for the Lord, Yahweh of Armies, has a sacrifice in the north country by the river Euphrates.
Go up into Gilead, and take balm, virgin daughter of Egypt. In vain do you use many medicines. There is no healing for you.
The nations have heard of your shame, and the earth is full of your cry; for the mighty man has stumbled against the mighty, they both fall together.”
The word that Yahweh spoke to Jeremiah the prophet, how that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon should come and strike the land of Egypt.
“Declare in Egypt, publish in Migdol, and publish in Memphis and in Tahpanhes: say, ‘Stand up, and prepare; for the sword has devoured around you.’
Why are your strong ones swept away? they didn’t stand, because Yahweh pushed them.
He made many to stumble, yes, they fell on one another: and they said, ‘Arise, and let us go again to our own people, and to the land of our birth, from the oppressing sword.’
They cried there, ‘Pharaoh king of Egypt is but a noise; he has let the appointed time pass by.’
“As I live,” says the King, whose name is Yahweh of Armies, “surely like Tabor among the mountains, and like Carmel by the sea, so shall he come.
You daughter who dwells in Egypt, furnish yourself to go into captivity; for Memphis shall become a desolation, and shall be burned up, without inhabitant.
“Egypt is a very beautiful heifer; but destruction out of the north has come. It has come.

Also her hired men in the middle of her are like calves of the stall; for they also are turned back. They have fled away together. They didn’t stand, for the day of their calamity has come on them, the time of their visitation.
It’s sound will go like the serpent; for they shall march with an army, and come against her with axes, as wood cutters.
They shall cut down her forest,” says Yahweh, “though it can’t be searched; because they are more than the locusts, and are innumerable.
The daughter of Egypt shall be disappointed; she shall be delivered into the hand of the people of the north.”
Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says: “Behold, I will punish Amon of No, and Pharaoh, and Egypt, with her gods, and her kings; even Pharaoh, and those who trust in him.

I will deliver them into the hand of those who seek their lives, and into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and into the hand of his servants. Afterwards it shall be inhabited, as in the days of old,” says Yahweh.

“But don’t you be afraid, Jacob my servant, neither be dismayed, Israel; for, behold, I will save you from afar, and your offspring  from the land of their captivity. Jacob will return, and will be quiet and at ease. No one will make him afraid.

Don’t be afraid, O Jacob my servant,” says Yahweh; “for I am with you; for I will make a full end of all the nations where I have driven you; but I will not make a full end of you, but I will correct you in measure, and will in no way leave you unpunished.”

footnotes.content: Jeremiah's word reaches beyond Judah now—to the nations themselves. The Lord speaks first to His own prophet, then through him to empires that thought themselves beyond His care. What a comfort to know that the God who calls us also calls the world to account.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Carchemish by the Euphrates—that great battle where Egypt's army met Babylon's king and fell. Jeremiah names the place, the year, the king, the defeat. Truth is stubborn; it leaves witnesses and dates. So does the word of the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The officers bark orders: bucklers, shields, draw near! But Jeremiah's audience already knows the ending—the word has gone out, the Lord has spoken. All that armor, all that courage, meets a will that cannot be resisted. Pride goes before the fall.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Polish the spears, harness the horses, stand tall in your helmets. See how urgent the command? Yet urgency itself can be a form of fear. The Lord works in His time, not in panic, not in the feverish scramble of human anxiety.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Dismayed. Turned backward. Beaten down. Fleeing in haste. This is not battle—this is rout, collapse, the mighty ones running without looking back. Jeremiah speaks as an eyewitness to what the Lord has already seen and decreed. 'Terror is on every side,' He says, and so it comes to pass.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The swift cannot outrun the Lord's purpose. The mighty have nowhere to hide. North by the Euphrates—the place they thought was their stronghold becomes the place of their stumbling and fall. We learn slowly that all power is borrowed, all strength is held in His hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Nile in flood—Egypt's pride, Egypt's glory, a natural wonder. Yet here Jeremiah asks in wonder himself: 'Who is this?' as if to say, 'Do you think your rivers and your monuments are a match for the God of hosts?' The Lord speaks through the very metaphor that Egypt holds dear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Egypt boasts like the flooding Nile: 'I will rise up, I will cover the earth, I will destroy cities.' Listen to that pride! The same 'I will' that Satan whispers. The Lord lets such words be spoken and then answers with silence—and the world moves on.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Call to arms: horses, chariots, mighty men, Cush, Put, Ludim—a vast coalition, nations gathered in pride. Yet the prophet has already witnessed their defeat. In God's eyes, what looks like overwhelming force to us is already dust. This is Jeremiah's hard mercy: he lets them marshal their armies knowing what comes next.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sword devours. Blood satisfies its hunger. The Lord calls this day 'a day of vengeance,' and His armies have work to do north by the Euphrates. It is terrible and true: the God of grace is also the God of judgment, and when His time comes, the work is thorough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Go to Gilead for balm—Egypt grasps at remedies, at healing, at fixes. But there is no physician for a wound that the Lord Himself has struck. In vain do they seek their medicines. Only He can heal what He has broken, and He does so only on His terms.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The earth is full of their cry. The nations hear of their shame. When great powers fall, all the world watches and learns. Here lies a mercy in disguise: the Lord lets failure teach what words often cannot. Humiliation, at least, is honest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now Jeremiah speaks again: Nebuchadnezzar is coming to strike Egypt. The word itself has two parts—first the preparation and the fall, now the agent of judgment is named. Babylon's king shall come, not by accident or fortune, but because the Lord has appointed him. History moves by the breath of God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Migdol, Memphis, Tahpanhes—cities named, a warning broadcast from place to place. The prophet calls the watchmen to cry out in the streets, to declare what is coming. Yet often when judgment approaches, ears grow deaf and hearts grow proud. The warning goes out; the people ignore it at their peril.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Why are the strong swept away? Because the Lord pushed them. No mystery, no luck—the reason is given plainly. The strongest man in the world is weak before the breath of God. There is a humility in accepting this truth, and in that humility lies peace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Soldiers stumble, fall on one another, cry out to go home. War undoes itself—man after man wants only to return to his birth-land, to flee the oppressing sword. The soldier's deepest wish is peace. How strange that we choose war to begin with.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Pharaoh is but a noise'—his own soldiers say it. When the appointed time passes unused, when a king fails to act, the people see through him. Empty authority reveals itself in crisis. A mighty name spoken in a small voice becomes a jest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As I live—the Lord swears by Himself, for there is none greater. Tabor among the mountains, Carmel by the sea—landmarks of power and majesty. Yet the Lord, in His coming, surpasses even these grand sights. His presence is more towering than any peak, more vast than any shoreline.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The daughter dwelling in Egypt is told to prepare for captivity. The language is gentle—'furnish yourself'—yet the word is hard. Memphis will become a desolation. Sometimes the Lord speaks plainly about what must come, so that there is no excuse for blindness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Egypt is a beautiful heifer. But beauty cannot stand against destruction coming from the north. There is something tender in the image—the prophet does not mock Egypt's loveliness, only names what comes. Judgment does not require us to deny what is good; it comes nonetheless.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hired men, stalled calves, soldiers turning back in flight—Egypt's armies scatter like cattle. The day of their visitation has come; no more can they hide or bargain. When the Lord's time arrives, preparations matter little.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sound of invasion is like a serpent creeping—axes swing, woodcutters strip the forest. The enemy comes methodically, relentlessly, cutting away everything that stood. Perhaps we hear in this a picture of how judgment clears away what has grown too wild, too tall, too proud.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Her forest will be cut down, though it cannot be searched—so great is the army that it cannot be counted. Like locusts, innumerable, they come. The numbers themselves speak: when the Lord sends judgment, it is thorough. There is no corner left untouched.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Egypt shall be disappointed—her hopes shall fail. She shall be delivered into the hand of the people of the north. The sentence is plain and final. The Lord does not mock or jeer; He simply speaks what will be, and watches it come to pass.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Amon of No, Pharaoh, Egypt, her gods, her kings—all shall be punished. The Lord names them all, spares none. Even the gods that Egypt has trusted in will fall. Idols cannot stand against the Lord of hosts; they crumble like dust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Into the hands of Nebuchadnezzar they are delivered. Yet hear the mercy hidden in judgment: 'Afterwards it shall be inhabited, as in the days of old.' The Lord destroys, but He does not destroy forever. After the night comes morning. After exile comes restoration.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But you, Jacob—the Lord turns now to His own people. 'Don't be afraid.' While Egypt falls, Israel hears a different word: I will save you from afar. Your offspring shall return. You will be quiet and at ease. This is the heart of God: to His scattered children, He promises not judgment but homecoming.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in these words: 'I am with you. I will not make a full end of you, but I will correct you in measure.' The God who brings judgment also brings presence. He corrects, yes—but in measure, with purpose, never abandoning His own. Across the centuries, His people still hear this promise in their darkest hours.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
